## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Loka Sutta* ("The World", Iti 112; It 4.13, PTS It 121) is a discourse in the *Catukkanipāta* of the *Itivuttaka*. The text sets forth the worldly dimensions comprehended by the Buddha and the distinctive spiritual attainments that entitle him to be known as the Tathāgata. It culminates in verses celebrating the Tathāgata as the tamed, peaceful, and liberated sage who liberates others [Levman 2014]. In a study of Buddhist verse style and Middle Indo-Aryan phonetics, Bryan Geoffrey Levman analyzes these lines (*danto damayataṁ seṭṭho santo samayataṁ isi / mutto mocayataṁ aggo tiṇṇo tārayataṁ varo*), noting the composer's deliberate use of sonorous parallel structures and causative participial forms [Levman 2014]. In doctrinal studies, the sutta is cited as an early canonical authority affirming that the Tathāgata truly speaks and expounds the Dhamma, a passage highlighted by Louis de La Vallée Poussin to contrast early Buddhist understandings of the Buddha with Madhyamaka perspectives [Tillemans 1992].
